# Layout

Figma: [Layout](https://www.figma.com/design/a7Z956YZy9n6f9uz5DK16Y?node-id=69-884)

The rules for how content is arranged on a screen - spacing rhythm, sizing scale, breakpoints, grid columns, and container widths. Safqah is Flutter mobile-first, so this page leans toward mobile patterns (safe areas, gesture zones, native chrome) while documenting tablet and desktop for completeness.

## Layout Overview

Layout is the spatial structure of an interface - how much space sits between elements, how containers are sized, where content can flow, and how the system adapts across screen widths. Syntropy's layout system is built around a strict 4px base unit, which scales up in multiples (4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 48, 64...) to create a predictable rhythm.

- Spacing - 11 semantic tokens from space/none (0px) to space/5xl (64px), governing gaps and padding
- Sizing - standard heights for buttons, inputs, app bars, and list items, all multiples of 4
- Breakpoints - mobile (default), tablet, and desktop bands for responsive adaptation
- Grid - column counts and gutters per breakpoint, for screens that need a formal grid
- Safe areas - mobile-specific zones to avoid (status bar, notches, home indicator)
- Foldables - iPhone Duo adds a compact outer display (466 × 678) and a regular inner display (951 × 669). Design two size classes plus one table pose arrangement; see "Foldables & iPhone Duo" below.

> **Info:** Spacing is the most-used token in any design system. Get it right and the interface feels effortless. Get it wrong and every screen feels slightly off - even if users can't articulate why. Stick to the scale.

## Spacing Scale

Eleven semantic spacing tokens cover all gaps and padding in the system. The scale is non-linear - smaller increments at the bottom (where precision matters) and larger jumps at the top (where the difference between 32 and 48 is meaningful, but 32 vs 33 isn't).

| space/none | 0px |  | No gap - adjacent elements (toolbars, segmented controls) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| space/2xs | 2px |  | Hairline - borders between visually-tight elements |
| space/xs | 4px |  | Very tight - icon + adjacent label, status dot to text |
| space/sm | 8px |  | Tight - buttons to adjacent items, dense list rows |
| space/md | 12px |  | Default - most internal padding, between related items |
| space/lg | 16px |  | Comfortable - between sections, card padding |
| space/xl | 20px |  | Spacious - between distinct content blocks |
| space/2xl | 24px |  | Section breaks within a screen |
| space/3xl | 32px |  | Major section breaks, padding around heros |
| space/4xl | 48px |  | Page-level vertical padding, between unrelated sections |
| space/5xl | 64px |  | Maximum scale - hero margins, marketing layouts |

> **Tip:** The 4-8-12-16 cluster (xs/sm/md/lg) covers ~80% of all spacing decisions. When in doubt, pick md (12px) - it's the default for internal padding and most adjacent-element gaps.

## Sizing Reference

Standard heights for common UI elements. These aren't tokenized as Figma variables - they're conventions baked into each component. Designers don't set heights manually; they pick the right component variant and the height comes with it.

| Element | Compact | Default | Comfortable / Use case |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Button | 32px | 40px | 48px - primary CTAs, mobile-prominent actions |
| Input field | 40px | 48px | 56px - financial inputs, prominent forms |
| App bar / nav bar | 48px | 56px | 64px - mobile top bars (with status bar above) |
| Tab bar / bottom nav | 56px | 64px | 80px - bottom tab bar (with safe area below) |
| List item - single line | 44px | 56px | 64px - comfortable touch target |
| List item - two line | 56px | 72px | 80px - title + metadata pattern |
| List item - three line | 72px | 88px | 104px - title + description + metadata |
| FAB (floating action button) | 40px | 56px | 64px - extended FAB with label |
| Avatar | 24/32px | 40px | 64/80px - profile screens |
| Icon button | 32px | 40px | 48px - minimum 44×44 tap target |
| Modal / bottom sheet | auto-fit | auto-fit | max 90% screen height - mobile |

> **Tip:** Minimum tap target is 44×44 (Apple) / 48×48 (Google). Anything below that fails accessibility for users with motor impairments. The "Compact" sizes above are for visual density - but always include enough padding around them to hit the tap-target minimum.

## Breakpoints

Safqah is Flutter mobile-first - the primary canvas is the phone. Tablet and desktop are documented for completeness and for any future web admin tooling, but mobile patterns drive the design system.

| Breakpoint | Width range | Container max | Gutter | Columns | Primary devices |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| mobile (default) | 0 – 599px | fluid (100%) | 16px | 4 | iPhone / Android phones - Safqah's primary target |
| tablet | 600 – 1023px | 720px | 24px | 8 | iPad / Android tablets - limited Safqah use |
| foldable inner | 669 – 951px | 2 × 390px columns | 16px | 8 (even only) | iPhone Duo inner display - regular × regular, 84px vertical bar on the right, fold at the centre |
| desktop | 1024 – 1439px | 1200px | 32px | 12 | Web admin tools, future dashboards |
| wide | 1440px + | 1400px | 32px | 12 | Large displays - cap container, don't stretch |

> **Info:** These breakpoints match Material Design 3's window-size classes (Compact, Medium, Expanded, Large). Engineers reference them in Flutter via MediaQuery.of(context).size.width comparisons or the breakpoint constants in safqah/layout/breakpoints.dart.

## Container Widths & Padding

Content shouldn't span the full width of the screen on tablet or wider. Containers cap the maximum reading width and add horizontal padding so text and controls stay scannable. On mobile, content fills the available width minus the side padding.

| Mobile container | < 600px | Padding: 16px each side · Content fills remaining width |
| --- | --- | --- |
Content (fluid)

All Safqah mobile screens. Side padding is non-negotiable - never let content butt up against the screen edge.

| Tablet container | 600 – 1023px | Padding: 24px each side · Max content width: 720px (centered) |
| --- | --- | --- |
Content (720px max)

Tablet screens cap at 720px even if the screen is wider. Don't stretch line lengths past comfortable reading.

| Desktop container | 1024 – 1439px | Padding: 32px each side · Max content width: 1200px (centered) |
| --- | --- | --- |
Content (1200px max)

Desktop web (future admin tools). Generous side margins so content doesn't feel cramped.

| Wide container | ≥ 1440px | Padding: 32px each side · Max content width: 1400px (centered) |
| --- | --- | --- |
Content (1400px max)

Large monitors. Don't stretch content further - cap and center. The page background takes the leftover space.

## Stack vs Grid

Two layout patterns cover 95% of screens: Stack (one direction - vertical or horizontal flow) and Grid (two-dimensional, fixed columns). In Figma terms, both use auto-layout. The difference is whether you're arranging items along one axis or two.

Stack

One-direction flow - items follow each other vertically or horizontally with consistent gaps.

Use when:

• Forms (label + input + helper text vertically)

• Lists (rows of cards, list items)

• Page sections (header → content → actions)

• Inline groups (icon + text side by side)

Grid

Two-dimensional - items arranged in rows and columns, usually equal-width cells.

Use when:

• Image galleries (photo grids, deal cards)

• Numerical dashboards (KPI tiles)

• Selectable options (color pickers, icon pickers)

• Comparative data (4 quadrants of stats)

> **Tip:** If the items don't need to be equal-width, use Stack with wrap enabled instead of Grid. True grids should have items of equal weight (visual mass). Mixed-size content in a "grid" usually means you wanted a Stack.

## Safe Areas (Mobile)

Modern phones have screen regions that aren't safe for interactive content - status bars, notches, dynamic islands, home indicators, and gesture areas. Designers must respect these zones or critical UI gets clipped, obscured, or interpreted as a system gesture.

Status bar zone - 44–54px

Safe content zone

Home indicator zone - 34px

Status bar / Dynamic Island

Top 44–54px on iOS, 24–48px on Android. Never place tappable content here - the OS reserves it for clock, battery, indicators. App bars sit BELOW this zone.

Safe content zone

The middle area where all interactive content lives. Modal sheets, lists, hero content, and primary actions go here.

Home indicator zone (iOS)

Bottom 34px on iPhones with Face ID. iOS interprets swipes here as system gestures - don't place buttons or scrollable content directly on it. Tab bars and bottom sheets need built-in bottom padding to clear this zone.

Edge gesture zones

The leftmost 12px (and rightmost on iOS) trigger system back/swipe gestures. Don't place horizontal scrollers or swipeable cards in this zone without explicit testing.

Vertical bar and lens (iPhone Duo)

On the outer display and the inner landscape display the status bar, camera lens and system bars live in an 84px strip on the right edge. It stays on the right in Arabic. Keep content and taps left of it (382px usable on the outer display, 867px on the inner) and never under the 96 × 96 lens corner.

> **Warning:** In Flutter, always wrap top-level scaffolds with SafeArea or use Scaffold's built-in safe area handling. Don't manually pad for safe areas - device sizes change, OS updates change them, and hardcoded paddings break on new hardware.

## Foldables & iPhone Duo

iPhone Duo (iOS 27.1, ships 23 Oct 2026) adds a second, foldable inner display. We do not design per pose: we design two size classes (compact on the outer display, regular on the inner display) plus one optional table-pose arrangement, and every pose keeps the same content, functionality and hierarchy. Chrome comes from the "iOS and iPadOS 27" library, never drawn by hand.

| Frame code | Size (pt) | Size class | Bars | When to build |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| OUTER | 466 × 678 | Compact W, Regular H | Vertical bar, right side (84 pt). Usable content 382 pt | Always. Closed device, portrait. Single column, same as the phone layout minus 166 pt of height |
| INNER | 951 × 669 | Regular W, Regular H | Vertical bar, right side (84 pt). Usable content 867 pt | Always. Open flat, landscape. Split, reflow or right-column layouts; never a stretched single column |
| TABLE | 669 × 951 | Regular W, Regular H | Horizontal bars (84 pt top toolbar, floating tab bar 409 × 95) | Always. Seated on a surface, folded on a horizontal hinge at y 476. Glanceable content top, controls bottom |
| INNER-BOOK | 951 × 669 + vertical fold band | Regular W, Regular H | As INNER | Only when interactive elements (sheets, alerts, menus, CTAs, grids) would land on the vertical fold at x 475 |
| INNER-PORTRAIT | 669 × 951 | Regular W, Regular H | Horizontal bars | Only when the screen is used flat in portrait and its bars differ from TABLE |
| OUTER-LANDSCAPE | 678 × 466 | Compact W, Compact H | Vertical bar (84 pt) | Only for viewers realistically used with the closed phone rotated (documents, charts) |
| SPLIT-VIEW | about half of INNER, minus the system divider | Compact W | Controls move to the left edge when Safqah is the left app | Tier 1 screens only. Any screen may be given an arbitrary width at any moment |

| Region or chrome | Measurement | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vertical bar | 84 pt wide, flush right | Hardware fixed. It stays on the right in Arabic too, so right insets carry bar + margin while left insets do not. Back or Close first, then the prominent action. 48 × 48 items, 12 pt side padding, 12 pt gap |
| Outer display lens | 96 × 96, top right corner | Keep-out. Nothing interactive under it. The Dynamic Island grows vertically along the bar for Live Activities |
| Inner camera region | Active only while the camera runs | UI moves aside. Matters for ID capture, selfie and certificate scan |
| Fold keep-out | Not published (placeholder duo/fold/keepout) | Drawn as a dashed guide at x 475 (book) or y 476 (table) until Device Hub gives the real width. Prefer even column counts, never 3 columns |
| Top title row | 84 pt tall in vertical-bar layouts | Title only, starting at x 20, plus a 44 × 48 camera reserved region at its right end. Arabic title alignment is an open question |
| Keyboard, outer portrait | 466 × 286 at y 392 | iOS 27 library "Keyboard", Display Outer, Orientation Portrait. Spans under the bar |
| Keyboard, inner landscape | 951 × 275 at y 394 | Library "Keyboard", Display Inner, Orientation Landscape |
| Keyboard, inner portrait | 669 × 361 at y 590 | Library "Keyboard", Display Inner, Orientation Portrait. Fills the bottom half in TABLE, so the active field must live in the top half |
| Sheets | Outer: 450 wide, 8 pt inset, own 76 pt bar. Inner folded: 468 × 587 in one half | Outer sheets also move controls to the side. Inner sheets are centered and slide off the fold when folded. BottomSheet (06c) needs these variants |
| Biometrics | Touch ID, not Face ID | Every Face ID string, glyph and illustration must branch by biometry type |
| OUTER · 466 × 678 Closed, portrait. Content column 382 pt, vertical bar and lens on the right. Keyboard 286 pt. | INNER · 951 × 669 Open flat, landscape. Right column 390 pt holds the form, left half reserved; the fold at x 475 stays clear. | TABLE · 669 × 951 Seated on a surface, folded at y 476. Glanceable content top, controls and keyboard bottom, horizontal bars. |
Apple's rules (HIG, Designing for iPhone Duo)

- Size classes, not poses: build compact (OUTER) and regular (INNER). TABLE is a rearrangement of INNER, never a reduced feature set. No fixed widths or metrics tied to one screen.
- Three honest inner patterns: split view (list + detail, hierarchy unchanged), reflow (one stack becomes two even columns) or right column. Sidebar navigation is not needed for a 3-tab app.
- Vertical bar: symbols go vertical, text-only items stay horizontal, segmented controls stay in the nav bar, counts become badges, an item carrying a money amount stays in content. Every item needs a title for overflow, and overflow runs bottom to top by priority.
- RTL: the bar is aligned to the hardware and does not mirror. Content mirrors, insets are asymmetric, and the Back symbol lives at the top of the bar. EN check frames exist to prove only content mirrors.
- Fold displacement: buttons, sheets, alerts, menus and CTAs move away from the fold, scrolling content does not. Move related elements together. Book pose alerts go to the trailing side; table pose puts readable content top and taps bottom.
- Continuity: opening or closing mid-task must preserve selection, scroll position, form values, keyboard focus and OTP countdowns. Closing from a split shows the deepest level with Back to the list.
- Content position: offset to the safe-area insets by default. Full-display centering only for immersive, non-interactive moments (success celebration, credential card hero).
Safqah conventions (from the KYC and account recovery adaptations)

- Every Duo frame is a duplicate of the production 390 pt frame with layout changed only, built on auto layout: OUTER = [content | bar], INNER = [left pane | 390 pt right column | bar], TABLE = [top bar 84 | top region 392 | bottom region]. Keyboard, lens, fold guide and background art are absolute.
- Rhythm on the 4/8 grid: 24 pt top padding, 24 pt illustration to title, 16 pt between form rows (8 pt when the block already carries padding), CTA pinned with space-between. Tap targets stay 44 pt or more with 8 pt between them.
- INNER: progress bar at the top of the right column, illustration above the title, then form and CTA in production order. The left half stays free for illustrations. Long forms that would scroll reflow into two columns (questions 1 to 5 right, 6 to 9 and CTA left).
- Keyboard states: the keyboard is full width; the CTA sits above it; the column lifts, then the illustration scales, then gaps tighten. An illustration that would fall under 48 pt is hidden and noted on the header card. In TABLE the CTA joins the top column when the 114 pt between fold and keyboard cannot hold it.
- Chrome: iOS 27 library instances only (Keyboard, Status bar - iPhone Duo, Outer Display Lens, Vertical Bar, Sheets). Header symbols (Back, Help, Language, Logout) become 48 pt bar items; the production header stays horizontal in TABLE. Toasts sit top centre of the content column. Dark screens use white chrome.
- Naming: [Flow] / [Screen] / [FrameCode] / [State] / [Lang]. AR first; EN only for the listed EN check screens. Each screen gets a Screen details card placed from its real height (row y minus card height minus 32).

> **Warning:** Automatic vertical bars, displacement and fold-aware sheets only come from native navigation containers. Syntropy AppBar (06a) and TabBar (06b) are custom, and the Flutter bridge means none of this is free: every bar move, displacement and overflow rule in this section must be implemented and annotated by hand until engineering confirms native containers.

> **Tip:** Compose INNER from OUTER modules: half of the inner display is about 475 pt, close to the 466 pt outer width, so a 382 to 470 pt module fits both. Verify all placeholder measurements (fold keep-out, bar width, inner points) in Xcode 27.1 Device Hub before final specs.

### Why layout matters

Layout is the invisible structure that holds an interface together. When users say a screen "feels right" - clear, balanced, easy to scan - they're responding to its layout. When they say something feels "off" but can't articulate what, layout is usually the culprit. Misaligned elements, inconsistent gaps, cramped padding - these subliminal frictions accumulate into a sense of amateur work.

In a fintech product, layout is also about trust. Users assume that a company with sloppy spacing is sloppy with money. Tight, intentional layout signals "this team pays attention to details." Loose, drifting layout signals the opposite - even when every other aspect of the screen is perfect.

Syntropy's layout system is built to eliminate ambiguous decisions. Eleven spacing tokens, four breakpoints, standard heights for every common component - designers don't debate "should this be 11px or 12px?" because 11 isn't in the system. The constraint is the system's job; expression is the designer's.

### Choosing the right spacing

Spacing is the most-used token in the system. Every padding, every gap, every margin reaches for one of the 11 space/* tokens. Picking the wrong one is rarely fatal but consistently picking the wrong one is what makes interfaces feel cheap.

| Col 1 | Col 2 |
| --- | --- |
| Default to space/md (12px) when uncertain | For most internal padding, list item gaps, and inline element separation, 12px is the right answer. It's tight enough to feel structured, generous enough to read clearly. If you don't have a specific reason to pick something else, pick md. |
| Pair tight content with tight spacing | Dense interfaces (data tables, transaction lists, compact forms) need smaller gaps - sm (8px) between rows, xs (4px) within a row. Wide-open interfaces (marketing screens, onboarding) need bigger gaps - lg/xl/2xl. Match spacing to content density. |
| Group related content with smaller spacing | Items that belong together should have less space between them than items that don't. A form label sits 4px above its input (xs), but 16px below the previous field (lg). Spacing communicates grouping. |
| Avoid space/none unless needed | Adjacent elements with zero spacing are rare in practice - toolbars, segmented controls, joined buttons. For almost everything else, give content at least 4px of breathing room. Zero-gap layouts are easy to over-use. |

> **Tip:** When debugging cramped layouts, increase spacing by one step (md → lg → xl) and see if it helps. When debugging fragmented layouts (content feels disconnected), decrease spacing by one step. Spacing changes are usually the right fix, not size or color changes.

### Density vs comfort

Every screen makes a density tradeoff - show more content per screen, or give each piece of content more space to breathe. Both extremes have value; the wrong choice for the context is what hurts users.

| Col 1 | Col 2 |
| --- | --- |
| High density for power users | When users are scanning rapidly through lots of data - transaction lists, portfolio holdings, deal pipelines - pack content tightly. Use sm (8px) gaps, smaller font sizes (body/13 or body/14), compact button heights (32px). Density rewards scanning speed. |
| Low density for first-time users | Onboarding, account setup, KYC steps - these moments need generous breathing room. Big buttons (48px+), spacious gaps (lg/xl), larger font sizes (body/16+). Low density reduces cognitive load when users are unfamiliar with the flow. |
| Default to medium density for fintech | Safqah's investor product sits in the middle. Users need to scan returns, deal cards, and statuses quickly (favoring density) but also need confidence in the numbers they're reading (favoring comfort). Medium density - md (12px) gaps, body/14 text, 40px buttons - is the right default. |
| Density toggles are usually overkill | Some products offer "compact view" toggles. For a single-segment audience like Safqah's investors, this is over-engineered. Pick one density that works for the dominant user state and apply it everywhere. Don't make users configure their density. |

### RTL implications for layout

When the interface flips to Arabic, layout reverses horizontally. This affects more than just text direction - it changes which side icons sit on, where progress bars fill from, and which corner radius applies to leading vs trailing edges. Designing in LTR but shipping in both requires explicit attention to this from the start.

| Col 1 | Col 2 |
| --- | --- |
| Use logical properties, not physical ones | In Figma and Flutter, prefer "leading" / "trailing" over "left" / "right" wherever possible. A button with leading padding 16 reads as 16px on the left in English and 16px on the right in Arabic. A button with paddingLeft: 16 stays on the LEFT in both - usually wrong. |
| Test every screen in Arabic mode | It's tempting to design only in English and "trust the flip." But some layouts break in RTL - directional icons (arrows, chevrons) need explicit mirroring, multi-column layouts may need different column order, numerical alignment changes. Always toggle the mode and review. |
| Numbers stay LTR within RTL | Even in Arabic mode, numerical values read left-to-right (12,500 SAR, not 005,21 SAR). Currency symbols position differently per locale (12,500 SAR vs ر.س 12,500). Use Flutter's NumberFormat and Locale-aware widgets - don't hardcode positions. |
| Spacing tokens work the same in both modes | space/md is 12px in both English and Arabic. The values don't flip - only the direction they're applied does. This is one fewer thing to worry about, as long as you use logical spacing properties. |

### Anti-patterns (Don't do this)

Layout mistakes that compound silently across screens.

> **Don't:** Don't use raw pixel values. If you write padding: 14px anywhere, you're breaking the system. Even "I just need 15px" is a smell - pick the nearest token (md = 12 or lg = 16) and adjust the design instead.

> **Don't:** Don't nest auto-layout without thinking. Deeply nested auto-layout frames are hard to maintain and slow Figma down. Most layouts need 2-3 levels max. Flatten where you can.

> **Don't:** Don't mix horizontal alignment within a stack. If items in a vertical stack are left-aligned, all of them should be left-aligned. Mixing left, center, and right alignment within a single stack creates visual chaos.

> **Don't:** Don't fight the breakpoint system. If a screen needs a custom container width of 950px because "1024 feels too wide," the design is fighting the system. Either redesign within the existing breakpoints or propose a system change - don't one-off it.

> **Don't:** Don't use spacing to communicate hierarchy alone. Spacing tells users what's grouped - it doesn't make something more important. To emphasize, change weight, size, or color. Then adjust spacing to support the hierarchy you've already set.

> **Don't:** Don't skip safe-area handling on mobile. Hardcoded top padding "to clear the status bar" breaks on devices with bigger notches. Always use Flutter's SafeArea widget - never hardcode.

> **Don't:** Don't treat tablet as "big mobile." Tablet layouts should rearrange content (sidebars, two-column lists, split views), not just stretch mobile patterns across more pixels. If the design is identical at 600px and 900px, you're probably leaving usability on the table.
